blocks.text: **The problem.** Build a queue on top of an array. Support `enqueue(x)` (add x at the back), `dequeue()` (remove and return the front item, or **-1** if the queue is empty), `front()` (return the front item, or **-1** if empty), `isEmpty()` and `size()`. The queue must keep working however many items pass through it.

blocks.alt: An array holding 5, 8 and 3 in slots 0 to 2, with three free slots after them. The front of the queue, where items leave, is slot 0. The back, where items join, is slot 2, the last used slot. Adding at the end of an array is cheap; removing from slot 0 is not.

blocks.code:
enqueue(10)   enqueue(20)   front()   -> 10
dequeue()     -> 10         size()    -> 1
dequeue()     -> 20         dequeue() -> -1  (empty)

blocks.text: Enqueue is easy on any array: append at the end. The whole problem is the **front**. Items leave from the start of the array, and the start is exactly where an array is slow to change.
1. Brute force: the front is always index 0

Keep the front at index 0. Dequeue takes `data[0]` and then **shifts every other item one place left**, so the next item becomes the new `data[0]`. This is what JavaScript's `shift()` and Python's `list.pop(0)` do behind the scenes.

blocks.alt: Dequeue with the front at index 0. The array holds 5, 8, 3, 6. 5 leaves, then 8, 3 and 6 each shift one slot left, giving 8, 3, 6.

elements.text: dequeue: 5 leaves, then everything shifts left
elements.originalText: dequeue: 5 leaves, then everything shifts left

blocks.text: **enqueue O(1); dequeue O(n); space O(n).** Emptying a queue of n items costs n + (n − 1) + … + 1 ≈ n²/2 moves — far too slow for a busy queue.

Why move the items at all? Keep a `head` index pointing at the front item. Dequeue reads `data[head]` and moves `head` one step right — nothing shifts. The live queue is everything from `head` to the end.

blocks.alt: The array holds 5, 8, 3, 6, 2, 9. Slots 0 to 2 have been served and are greyed out; head points at slot 3, which holds 6. Dequeue is just head++, O(1). But the served slots are never used again.

blocks.text: There's a catch: the slots before `head` are **dead** — served, but still taking up room. A queue that sees a million items in its life but never holds more than ten at once would still keep a million-slot array. The version below at least starts afresh whenever the queue becomes **empty**, but a busy queue that is never quite empty still grows forever.
**Every operation O(1).** But space is **O(items enqueued since the queue was last empty)** instead of O(items in the queue now).
3. Best solution: a circular array that doubles

Reuse the dead slots. Treat the array as a **ring**: after the last slot comes slot 0 again. Keep `head` (the front's index) and `count` (how many items are stored). The back is then found, not stored: the next free slot is `(head + count) % capacity`. Both ends move forward and **wrap around** with `% capacity`, so a slot freed by a dequeue is reused by a later enqueue.

blocks.alt: A ring of 4 slots. Slot 2 holds 7 and is the front, so head is 2. Slot 3 holds 8. Slot 0 holds 9: the back wrapped around from slot 3 to slot 0. Slot 1 is free. With count 3, the next free slot is (2 + 3) % 4 = 1.

blocks.text: Why `count` and not a `tail` index? With only head and tail, an **empty** queue and a **full** one look identical — in both, head equals tail. Keeping `count` tells them apart. (The other common fix is to always leave one slot empty.)

When every slot is in use, the array can't take one more item. Allocate one **twice as big** and copy the items in **front-first** order, which unwraps the ring: the front lands at index 0. Doubling is O(n), but it happens so rarely that enqueue is still **O(1) amortized** — the same argument as for a growing array stack.

blocks.alt: Growing a full ring. The ring of 4 holds 9, 10, 7, 8 with the front at slot 2. It is copied front first into 8 slots: 7, 8, 9, 10, followed by four free slots, and head becomes 0.

blocks.caption: Watch head wrap past the end, then the array double. Served values stay greyed out until a later enqueue overwrites them.

blocks.text: **enqueue O(1) amortized; dequeue, front, isEmpty and size O(1); space O(n)** — the array is never more than twice the number of items it holds. This is how Java's `ArrayDeque` works inside.

blocks.alt: Brute force: dequeue O(n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(1) time, O(items ever) space. Best: O(1) amortized time, O(n) space.

items: **dequeue and front on an empty queue** — both must return -1, at the start and again after the queue empties.
**Wrapping** — enqueue 3, dequeue 2, enqueue 3 more: the back passes the end of the array and continues at slot 0.
**Growing while wrapped** — fill the ring when `head` isn't 0. The copy must start at `head`, not at slot 0, or the order breaks.
**Many laps** — a queue that never holds more than 2 items but sees 100: `head` goes round the ring many times, and the array never grows.
**Storing -1** — returning -1 for "empty" is ambiguous if -1 is a real item. Check `isEmpty()` first, or return a separate flag.
**Design Circular Queue** (LeetCode 622) — a fixed capacity k: `enQueue` returns false when full instead of growing. Add `isFull()` (count === k) and `Rear()` (the slot `(head + count − 1) % k`).
**Design Circular Deque** (LeetCode 641) — add and remove at both ends: the front moves **backwards** with `(head − 1 + k) % k`.
**Moving Average from a Data Stream** — keep the last `size` values in a ring with a running sum; each new value overwrites the oldest.
**Queue on a linked list** — the next problem: no capacity, no wrapping, but a pointer per item.
